What exactly is the Krebs cycle?

blocks.x: The Krebs cycle — also called the Citric Acid Cycle or the Tricarboxylic Acid (TCA) Cycle — is a series of enzymatic reactions used by every aerobic living organism to generate cellular energy. It works by oxidizing acetyl units (derived from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins) all the way down to carbon dioxide and water. It's named after biochemist Hans Adolf Krebs (1900–1981), who first described it.

Picture a busy central roundabout that every route in town eventually feeds into — trucks carrying carbohydrates, trucks carrying fats, trucks carrying proteins, all merging onto the same circular road. That's the Krebs cycle: the central metabolic pathway connecting almost every other individual metabolic pathway in the body. It's the final common oxidative route for carbohydrates, proteins, and fats alike.

Beyond just burning fuel, the Krebs cycle does two jobs at once: it supplies energy (ATP) and reduced coenzymes (FADH₂, NADH) for the electron transport chain, and it provides intermediates used to build other biomolecules — heme (porphyrins), nucleotide bases, and amino acids.

sections.title: Where does the Krebs cycle fit into cellular respiration?

blocks.x: <term d="The overall process by which biochemical energy from nutrients is converted into usable cellular energy (ATP).">Cellular respiration</term> is simply the process of generating energy (ATP) from the food we eat. It has three connected stages, all happening inside — or leading into — the <term d="The organelle where aerobic respiration takes place; contains the matrix where the Krebs cycle occurs.">mitochondrion</term>, specifically its inner compartment, the <term d="The innermost compartment of the mitochondrion, enclosed by the inner membrane, where the Krebs cycle enzymes are located.">matrix</term>.

blocks.cap: Glycolysis hands off pyruvate → the Krebs cycle strips off carbons and electrons → the electron transport chain cashes in those electrons for the bulk of the ATP.

blocks.title: Aerobic vs. anaerobic — the difference O₂ makes

blocks.x: With oxygen present, this full three-stage process runs: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + a large amount of energy. Without oxygen, cells fall back on anaerobic respiration: glucose → lactic acid + a much smaller amount of ATP. This is exactly why a footballer sprinting hard (glycolysis outrunning oxygen delivery) feels that burning sensation — the muscle has temporarily switched to the anaerobic, Krebs-cycle-bypassing route.

sections.title: Getting pyruvate ready to enter the cycle

blocks.x: Before the Krebs cycle can use it, pyruvate from glycolysis has to make a journey and undergo a transformation.
Pyruvate is translocated from the cytosol into the mitochondrial matrix, crossing the mitochondrial membranes via a dedicated pyruvate translocase.

Once inside, pyruvate is oxidatively decarboxylated to form Acetyl-CoA — releasing CO₂ and generating NADH. This reaction, run by the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase complex, is irreversible, and the Acetyl-CoA produced heads straight into the Krebs cycle.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — checking in your luggage before the flight

blocks.x: Pyruvate crossing into the mitochondrion is like passing through the departure gate before a flight — once you're through and your luggage (a carbon, as CO₂) is checked in, there's no casual walking back. It's a one-way, irreversible step, just like Acetyl-CoA formation.

blocks.cap: Three enzymes (E1, E2, E3) working as one assembly line to convert pyruvate into Acetyl-CoA.

blocks.x: The Pyruvate Dehydrogenase complex is built from 3 enzymes and 5 cofactors — Pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1) uses TPP; Dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase (E2) uses lipoamide and CoASH; Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3) uses FAD and NAD⁺. Each cofactor traces back to a specific vitamin: TPP ← Thiamine; NAD ← Niacin; FAD ← Riboflavin; CoA ← Pantothenic acid.
A rare disorder that raises blood lactate and pyruvate levels, potentially causing acidosis (which can be fatal in severe cases) and neurological problems.

A dietary lack of thiamine — commonly seen in alcoholics (malnourishment) or diets heavy in polished rice (husk removed, where thiamine is concentrated) — causes neurologic and cardiac problems. Without thiamine, pyruvate can't be oxidized, so it builds up in the blood. Activity of the cycle's two dehydrogenase enzymes drops, ATP production falls, and cellular function is impaired.

sections.title: One trip around the roundabout

blocks.x: Acetyl-CoA (2 carbons) joins oxaloacetate (4 carbons) to form citrate (6 carbons) — and over 8 steps, that citrate is gradually stripped back down to a 4-carbon molecule, releasing 2 CO₂ and capturing energy along the way, before regenerating oxaloacetate to start again.
Citrate synthase condenses Acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citrate (the same acid found in lemons and oranges), releasing CoA-SH. Strongly exergonic (ΔG'° = −32.2 kJ/mol).
Aconitase isomerizes citrate to isocitrate, via the intermediate cis-aconitate — simply rearranging atoms already present.
Isocitrate dehydrogenase oxidatively decarboxylates isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate, generating the cycle's 1st NADH and releasing the 1st CO₂.

The α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (structurally almost identical to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, using the same 5 coenzymes — TPP, CoASH, lipoic acid, NAD⁺, FAD) performs a second oxidative decarboxylation, forming succinyl-CoA and the 2nd NADH, releasing the 2nd CO₂.
Succinyl-CoA synthetase converts succinyl-CoA to succinate, directly generating a nucleoside triphosphate (GTP, convertible to ATP) via substrate-level phosphorylation.

Succinate dehydrogenase oxidizes succinate to fumarate, generating FADH₂. This enzyme is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and feeds electrons directly into the electron transport chain. Strongly and competitively inhibited by malonate.
Fumarase hydrates fumarate across its double bond to form malate — a highly stereospecific reaction (only one particular 3D configuration is produced).
Malate dehydrogenase oxidizes malate back to oxaloacetate, generating the cycle's 3rd NADH — and the roundabout is ready to accept another Acetyl-CoA.

blocks.title: Malonate — the impostor at the toll gate

blocks.x: Malonate closely resembles succinate in shape, so it competes for the same binding site on succinate dehydrogenase — exactly like a fake, similar-looking card jamming a toll gate's card slot. With malonate in the way, succinate piles up and FADH₂ production for the respiratory chain grinds to a halt.

blocks.title: Remember: this happens twice per glucose

blocks.x: Since glycolysis produces 2 pyruvate per glucose, and each pyruvate becomes one Acetyl-CoA, the Krebs cycle actually turns twice for every original glucose molecule — doubling all of the above: 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 GTP/ATP, and 4 CO₂ in total.

sections.title: How does the cell control the speed of the roundabout?

blocks.x: Three main factors regulate Krebs cycle activity:
The cycle simply can't run faster than its two starting materials — Acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate — are available.

Several steps are slowed by their own downstream products piling up — for example, isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited by ATP, while the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex is inhibited by succinyl-CoA and NADH.
A high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio signals the cell already has plenty of energy on hand, and multiple enzymes throughout the cycle respond by slowing down.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a roundabout with traffic sensors

blocks.x: Think of these three factors as different types of traffic control at the roundabout: substrate availability is simply how many vehicles are arriving; product inhibition is like downstream congestion signalling back to slow entry; and allosteric feedback (NADH/NAD⁺) is a citywide sensor system that senses "we already have plenty of energy stored" and dials the whole roundabout down.

blocks.title: Fast-acting override: covalent modification of PDH

blocks.x: Separately, the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase complex itself is switched on/off by phosphorylation: PDH kinase phosphorylates and inactivates it (favoured by ATP, acetyl-CoA, NADH — signs of abundant energy), while PDH phosphatase (activated by Ca²⁺) removes that phosphate and reactivates it. It's a fast, reversible on/off switch — like flipping a light switch rather than waiting for a whole new bulb to be installed.

blocks.title: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting one?

blocks.x: If a question asks for a single answer, it is isocitrate dehydrogenase — the rate-limiting enzyme of the Krebs cycle. It is activated by ADP and Ca²⁺ (signals that the cell is working hard and needs energy) and inhibited by ATP and NADH (signals that it already has plenty). Citrate synthase is the first and committed step, and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is the third control point — inhibited by its own products, succinyl-CoA and NADH. All three sit at irreversible steps, which is the general rule for where a pathway is controlled.
Each blocks one specific enzyme, and each is a favourite exam question:

items: Fluoroacetate (found in some plants, and used as a rodent poison) — converted in the cell into fluorocitrate, which blocks aconitase. Citrate then piles up.
Arsenite — binds the lipoic acid of α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (and of pyruvate dehydrogenase, which uses the same cofactor set).
Malonate — a competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase, because it looks like succinate.

blocks.x: Notice all three targets are dehydrogenase-type or iron-containing steps — exactly the points where the cycle harvests its reducing power.

Some individuals lack functional PDH phosphatase — meaning PDH stays permanently phosphorylated and inactive. Glucose then gets diverted to lactic acid instead, causing lactic acidosis, which disrupts tissue function — especially in the central nervous system.

sections.title: Not just a one-way burn — the cycle builds things too

blocks.x: The Krebs cycle is amphibolic — it serves both catabolic (breakdown, energy-releasing) and anabolic (biosynthetic, building-up) purposes at the same time.

blocks.cap: Krebs cycle intermediates feed directly into glucose, fatty acid, amino acid, purine, pyrimidine, and heme synthesis.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a roundabout that's also a marketplace

blocks.x: Most roundabouts just move traffic through. But imagine one that's also a busy marketplace — vehicles constantly peel off to drop goods (biosynthesis) while others merge in carrying fresh supplies (catabolism feeding the cycle). Oxaloacetate can peel off toward glucose or aspartate; α-ketoglutarate can peel off toward glutamate and its related amino acids; succinyl-CoA can peel off toward porphyrins and heme — all while the roundabout itself keeps turning to generate energy.

sections.title: Anaplerotic reactions — topping the roundabout back up

blocks.x: If biosynthesis keeps pulling intermediates out of the cycle, something has to replace them, or the whole roundabout would eventually run dry. That's the job of anaplerotic reactions — literally, "filling up" reactions.
Converts pyruvate directly to oxaloacetate, using ATP and CO₂ — the same reaction used in gluconeogenesis, now working in reverse-purpose to restock the cycle.
Converts phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to oxaloacetate as well — a second route into the same restocking pool.
Converts pyruvate directly to malate, using NADPH — restocking the cycle at a different point along the loop.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — keeping the depot stocked

blocks.x: Imagine a delivery fleet based at a roundabout depot, constantly sending vehicles out to different neighbourhoods carrying supplies (amino acids, heme, glucose). If nobody restocks the depot, it would eventually run empty and the roundabout traffic would stall completely. Anaplerotic reactions are the restocking trucks — bringing oxaloacetate and malate back into the depot so the roundabout can keep functioning even while constantly supplying other parts of the body.

sections.title: Key takeaways

items: The Krebs cycle (citric acid / TCA cycle) is the final common oxidative pathway for carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, running in the mitochondrial matrix.
Pyruvate must first be translocated into the mitochondrion and irreversibly converted to Acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex before entering the cycle.
One turn of the cycle produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP/ATP, and 2 CO₂ — doubled per glucose molecule, since glycolysis yields 2 pyruvate.
The cycle is regulated by substrate availability, product inhibition, and allosteric feedback (NADH/NAD⁺ ratio), plus fast on/off covalent control of the PDH complex.
The cycle is amphibolic — its intermediates double as starting materials for glucose, fatty acids, amino acids, purines, pyrimidines, and heme.
Anaplerotic reactions (pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, malic enzyme) replenish cycle intermediates drawn off for biosynthesis.

Key clinical links: thiamine deficiency (beriberi) impairs pyruvate oxidation; PDH deficiency and PDH phosphatase deficiency both cause lactic acidosis; malonate is a classic competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase.

steps.title: The Krebs Cycle, Step by Step

items.d: α-KG → Succinyl-CoA + CO2. Produces 1 NADH. Needs same 5 cofactors as PDH.
Succinate → Fumarate. Produces 1 FADH2 (directly in the inner membrane).
Malate → Oxaloacetate. Produces 1 NADH. Regenerates OAA to start again.
